etymology: Greek prizo, to saw in two. The Authorized Version's sawn asunder renders it at Hebrews 11:37, its only occurrence. Jewish tradition preserved in the Ascension of Isaiah held that the prophet Isaiah was executed this way under Manasseh.
biblical_def: They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword. The list is deliberately unbearable, and the writer does not soften a term in it. He has spent the chapter recounting what faith accomplished — kingdoms subdued, promises obtained, armies turned to flight — and then, without any break in the argument, he tells what faith cost. The same chapter, the same word, the same God. Sawn asunder stands out even among these because of its deliberateness; a man is not sawn in two in a riot but in an execution arranged and carried through. The church has always associated the phrase with Isaiah, whom Jewish tradition remembered as dying this way under Manasseh, though Scripture does not name him here. What Scripture does say is the thing that reframes every line of the list. These men did not escape; and of them it is written, Of whom the world was not worthy. The judgment on the executioners is delivered by the writer in a parenthesis, almost in passing, and it settles the question of who was actually being tried. The chapter ends by saying that none of them received the promise in their own lifetime, because God had provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under SAW and ASUNDER: cut with a saw; divided into parts; separated; parted.
webster_full: SAWN, pp. of saw. Cut with a saw; separated or divided by a saw.
SAW, n. A cutting instrument consisting of a blade or thin plate of iron or steel, with one edge dentated or toothed.
ASUNDER, adv. Apart; into parts; separately; in a divided state.
MARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defense of any cause; usually applied to one who suffers death in defense of the Christian religion.
PERSECUTION, n. The infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.
scriptures: They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Partly, whilst ye were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions; and partly, whilst ye became companions of them that were so used.
But we are not of them who draw back unto perdition; but of them that believe to the saving of the soul.
corruption_summary: Martyrdom is either sentimentalised into heroic spectacle or quietly dropped from the account of what faith may cost; Hebrews places it in the same list as the great deliverances, as the same faith with a different outcome.
corruption_paragraphs: A preaching that promises deliverance as the normal fruit of faith must do something with Hebrews 11:37, and what it usually does is skip it. The verse will not be skipped honestly, because the writer joins the two halves of his catalogue with no seam: the men who stopped the mouths of lions and the men who were sawn asunder are offered as one company. Faith is confidence in God's word about what is unseen and to come, and that confidence is equally present in the rescue and in the execution. Any doctrine that can only account for one half has not understood the chapter it is quoting from.

The opposite handling makes martyrdom a spectacle for admiration, remembered in stained glass at a comfortable distance and detached from ordinary obedience. Hebrews puts it to a different use. The writer immediately applies the whole catalogue to a congregation under pressure and wavering — we are not of them who draw back unto perdition — and reminds them of their own earlier endurance, when they were made a gazingstock and stood with those who were. The point of the roll call is not veneration of the dead but the steadying of the living, who are being asked to hold on in their own much smaller trial.
roots_summary: Greek prizo (G4249), to saw in two; lithazo (G3034), to stone; machaira (G3162), a sword; axios (G514), worthy.
roots_lines: Greek prizo (G4249) — to saw asunder; its only occurrence in Scripture.
Greek lithazo (G3034) — to stone; the death of Zechariah and of Stephen.
Greek machaira (G3162) — a sword; slain with the sword, as James the brother of John.
Greek axios (G514) — worthy, of equal weight; the world weighed and found wanting.
Greek teleioo (G5048) — to make perfect, to complete; they without us should not be made perfect.
usage: “they were sawn asunder” — execution, arranged and carried through.
“of whom the world was not worthy” — the verdict on the executioners.
“we are not of them who draw back” — the use the writer makes of it.

pos: v. (to receive and lodge a guest; to show hospitality)
etymology: Greek philoxenia, love of strangers, underlies the command; the verb xenizo means to receive as a guest. The English comes through French entretenir, from Latin inter and tenere, to hold among — to maintain, to keep company with.
biblical_def: Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares. The English word has drifted far from the Greek behind it. Philoxenia is love of strangers, and it means receiving into one's house a person who has no claim on it — a traveller, a refugee, someone unknown. It is not amusement and it is not the hosting of friends. The writer's argument is an appeal to memory: some have entertained angels unawares, which sends the reader straight to Abraham at the tent door in the heat of the day, saying to three strangers, My Lord, if now I have found favour in thy sight, pass not away, I pray thee, from thy servant. Abraham did not know who they were. That is the whole force of unawares. The command is issued to a suffering church, and its neighbours in the passage show the company it keeps: Let brotherly love continue stands immediately before it, and immediately after comes Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them. Hospitality here is not an ornament of the comfortable but a duty of a persecuted congregation toward people with nowhere to go — which in that century often meant fellow Christians driven out of their own towns. The phrase be not forgetful is realistic. This is precisely the duty that is not forgotten in principle and is constantly forgotten in practice.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to receive into the house and treat with hospitality; to receive and accommodate a guest; to keep in the mind.
webster_full: ENTERTAIN, v.t. To receive into the house and treat with hospitality, either at the table only, or with lodging also.
ENTERTAIN, v.t. To treat with conversation; to amuse or instruct by discourse.
ENTERTAIN, v.t. To keep in the mind; to harbor; to cherish; as, to entertain sentiments.
HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality.
STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one who is unknown.
scriptures: Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
And said, My Lord, if now I have found favour in thy sight, pass not away, I pray thee, from thy servant:
corruption_summary: Hospitality has been redefined as the entertaining of friends and the display of a home; Scripture commands the receiving of strangers who cannot repay, and lists it among the qualifications for eldership.
corruption_paragraphs: The English word has carried the practice with it. To entertain now means to host people one already knows, pleasantly, with the house presentable — an activity that can be graded and is therefore avoided by those who feel their house would grade poorly. Philoxenia is a different thing altogether: love of strangers, the receiving of someone with no claim and no means of returning the favour. The Lord made the distinction explicitly, telling a host not to call his friends or his rich neighbours, lest they bid him again and a recompense be made, but to call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind. A church that has only the first kind of hospitality has not a weaker version of the command; it has a different practice with the same name.

The second loss is that hospitality has been demoted to a personal temperament — something for those gifted at it. The New Testament treats it as a duty of all Christians and a requirement for elders, who must be given to hospitality and a lover of hospitality. Hebrews 13 sets it between brotherly love and remembering prisoners, which places it among the plain obligations of a church under pressure rather than among its refinements. Abraham's example is given precisely because he did not know whom he was receiving. The command is to open the door before the identity of the guest is known, which is the only kind of opening the word describes.
roots_summary: Greek philoxenia (G5381), love of strangers; xenos (G3581), a stranger or guest; lanthano (G2990), to escape notice; philadelphia (G5360), brotherly love.
roots_lines: Greek philoxenia (G5381) — love of strangers; the New Testament word for hospitality.
Greek xenos (G3581) — a stranger, an alien, a guest; the object of the command.
Greek lanthano (G2990) — to be hidden, to escape notice; rendered unawares.
Greek philadelphia (G5360) — brotherly love; the command standing immediately before.
Greek xenizo (G3579) — to receive as a guest, to lodge; used of Peter lodging with Simon a tanner.
usage: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” — the duty most often forgotten in practice.
“entertained angels unawares” — the door opened before the guest was known.
“Let brotherly love continue” — the company the command keeps.

etymology: Greek photizo, to give light, to enlighten, from phos, light. Latin illuminare, to light up. In the early church illumination became a standing term for the enlightening that accompanies conversion.
biblical_def: But call to remembrance the former days, in which, after ye were illuminated, ye endured a great fight of afflictions. The writer is steadying a congregation that is weakening, and his method is to send them back to their own beginning. After ye were illuminated dates the events he is about to recall: light came, and then the fight came. That order matters. Illumination in Scripture is not the reward of a long Christian life but the opening act of it — God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. The light is God's own giving, and it is given at the start. What followed, in their case, was not relief but a great fight of afflictions, and the writer describes it without euphemism: partly, whilst ye were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions; and partly, whilst ye became companions of them that were so used. They had been publicly shamed and had chosen to stand with others being publicly shamed. He recalls it to them because they had done it once, gladly, and were now in danger of drawing back. The Lord's own claim stands behind the whole figure: I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): enlightened; illustrated; made light; instructed; furnished with clear views.
webster_full: ILLUMINATE, v.t. To enlighten; to throw light on; to supply with light.
ILLUMINATE, v.t. To enlighten, as the mind; to cause to understand; to illustrate.
ILLUMINATED, pp. Enlightened; rendered light or luminous; instructed.
ILLUMINATION, n. The act of illuminating; that infusion of light into the mind which is derived from the Holy Spirit.
ENLIGHTEN, v.t. To make clear to the mind; to enable to see or comprehend truth; to instruct.
scriptures: But call to remembrance the former days, in which, after ye were illuminated, ye endured a great fight of afflictions;
Partly, whilst ye were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions; and partly, whilst ye became companions of them that were so used.
For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.
corruption_summary: Illumination is claimed either as a higher experience above ordinary faith or as a natural insight the mind achieves; Scripture makes it God's own shining into the heart at the outset of the Christian life.
corruption_paragraphs: Every generation produces a version of the two-tier Christian: the ordinary believer and the illuminated one, who has had a further experience the rest have not. The gnostic systems of the second century made this their whole architecture, and the pattern has recurred in mysticisms, perfectionisms, and second-blessing schemes since. Hebrews 10:32 uses the word of the entire congregation, at the beginning, as a plain date-marker for their conversion. Paul describes the same event as God commanding light to shine out of darkness in the heart — a creative act, done once, given to all who are Christ's.

The rationalist error empties the word from the other side, making illumination the mind's own arrival at religious insight through study or reflection. That cannot account for the language Scripture uses. The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness unto him, neither can he know them; the impediment is not a shortage of information. Illumination is the Spirit giving sight, which is why the Reformed tradition ties it to effectual calling and regeneration rather than to persuasion. It is also why the writer of Hebrews can use it as a fixed point in his readers' past — something that happened to them, which they can be called to remember.
roots_summary: Greek photizo (G5461), to enlighten; phos (G5457), light; athlesis (G119), a contest or fight; theatrizo (G2301), to make a spectacle of.
roots_lines: Greek photizo (G5461) — to give light, to enlighten; rendered illuminated here and enlightened elsewhere.
Greek phos (G5457) — light; the Lord's own title, the light of the world.
Greek athlesis (G119) — a contest, an athletic struggle; rendered fight of afflictions, its only occurrence.
Greek theatrizo (G2301) — to make a public spectacle; rendered made a gazingstock.
Greek lampo (G2989) — to shine; God hath shined in our hearts.
usage: “after ye were illuminated” — a date-marker, at the beginning.
“ye endured a great fight of afflictions” — what followed the light.
“hath shined in our hearts” — the same act, described by Paul.

etymology: Greek proorao, to see before or in front of. At Acts 2:25 the sense is not prediction but keeping continually in view — Peter renders the Hebrew of Psalm 16:8, I have set the LORD always before me.
biblical_def: For David speaketh concerning him, I foresaw the Lord always before my face, for he is on my right hand, that I should not be moved. Peter is preaching at Pentecost, and the verse he quotes is doing something the casual reader may miss. Foresaw here does not mean predicted; it renders a Hebrew phrase about constant orientation. David wrote, I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved. To have God always before one's face is to keep him in view in every circumstance, and the consequence David draws is stability — he is not moved, because his attention is fixed on the One who cannot be. Peter then uses the psalm for a purpose David could not fully have known. The psalm goes on: thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption. Peter argues that David died and was buried and his sepulchre is with us to this day, so that the psalm cannot terminate on David — and concludes: he seeing this before spake of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not left in hell, neither his flesh did see corruption. Two kinds of foresight meet in the passage. David kept the Lord before his face, and in doing so was given to see beforehand the resurrection of the Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under FORESEE: to see beforehand; to see or know an event before it happens; to have prescience of.
webster_full: FORESEE, v.t. To see beforehand; to see or know an event before it happens; to have prescience of, or foreknowledge of.
FORESAW, pret. of foresee. Saw beforehand.
PRESCIENCE, n. Foreknowledge; knowledge of events before they take place.
PROPHECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come.
CORRUPTION, n. The act of corrupting, or state of being corrupt or putrid; decomposition of animal substances.
scriptures: For David speaketh concerning him, I foresaw the Lord always before my face, for he is on my right hand, that I should not be moved:
I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.
Because thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.
He seeing this before spake of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not left in hell, neither his flesh did see corruption.
corruption_summary: Apostolic use of the Psalms is often dismissed as creative reapplication of texts that meant something else; Peter argues that the psalm cannot be exhausted by David and was spoken of the Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard critical account holds that Psalm 16 is a song of personal confidence with no messianic reference, and that Peter has reapplied it in a way its author never intended. Peter anticipates the objection and answers it by argument rather than assertion: David died, was buried, and his sepulchre is with us unto this day, therefore the words thou wilt not suffer thine Holy One to see corruption cannot be true of David. The psalm makes a claim that David's own tomb falsifies, which means the psalm was always looking past him. That is not reapplication; it is the reading the text requires, and Paul makes the same argument at Antioch.

The related loss is practical rather than academic. Because foresaw sounds like prediction, the first clause is read as though David were forecasting, and its actual counsel disappears. David is describing a habit — the LORD kept always before his face, at his right hand — and the stability he claims is the fruit of it. A believer who wants what the psalm promises is being told how it comes: not by a settled temperament but by a settled attention. The man who keeps God in view is the man who is not moved, and Peter quotes the whole sentence because the confidence and the resurrection hope belong together.
roots_summary: Greek proorao (G4308), to see before; saleuo (G4531), to shake or move; Hebrew shavah (H7737), to set or place; mowt (H4131), to be moved.
roots_lines: Greek proorao (G4308) — to see beforehand, to keep in view; rendered foresaw and seeing this before.
Greek saleuo (G4531) — to shake, to agitate; rendered moved.
Hebrew shavah (H7737) — to set, to place; I have set the LORD always before me.
Hebrew mowt (H4131) — to totter, to be moved; what David says he shall not be.
Greek diaphthora (G1312) — corruption, decay; what the Holy One did not see.
usage: “I foresaw the Lord always before my face” — constant orientation, not prediction.
“that I should not be moved” — the stability that follows the attention.
“he seeing this before spake of the resurrection” — Peter's argument.

pos: v. (to know beforehand; to set regard upon in advance)
etymology: Greek proginosko, to know before, from pro, before, and ginosko, to know. The Hebraic sense of know underlies Paul's usage: not bare awareness of facts but the setting of regard upon a person, as in you only have I known of all the families of the earth.
biblical_def: For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. The object of the verb decides the doctrine, and the object here is persons: whom he did foreknow, not what he foreknew about them. Paul is not saying God looked down the corridor of time, observed who would believe, and elected accordingly. He is saying God set his regard upon certain persons beforehand. That is the biblical sense of know throughout Scripture, and Amos uses it exactly so of a nation God had not merely observed but chosen: you only have I known of all the families of the earth. The chain Paul builds admits no leakage. Whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate; and whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified. Every group is the same group, carried through every link, and the last verb is in the past tense though glorification is still future — so certain is the outcome. Note also the end for which the predestination is made: conformity to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. Election terminates on the glory of Christ among a family of brethren, not on the comfort of the elect.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to have previous knowledge of; to foresee.
webster_full: FOREKNOW, v.t. To have previous knowledge of; to foresee.
FOREKNOWLEDGE, n. Knowledge of a thing before it happens; prescience.
PREDESTINATE, v.t. To predetermine or foreordain; to appoint or ordain beforehand by an unchangeable purpose.
ELECTION, n. The divine choice; predetermination of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy.
CONFORM, v.t. To make like in external appearance; to reduce to a likeness or correspondence in manners.
scriptures: For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: Grace unto you, and peace, be multiplied.
You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.
corruption_summary: Foreknowledge is widely made to mean God's advance observation of who would choose him, which reverses Paul's order; and open theism denies exhaustive divine foreknowledge outright.
corruption_paragraphs: The prescient-faith reading holds that God foreknew who would believe and elected them on that basis, making election a response to foreseen faith. Three things in the text stand against it. The object of foreknow is persons, not their future acts. The golden chain moves from foreknowledge to predestination to calling to justification with the same company throughout, so that faith appears as a fruit of the call rather than its cause. And Paul had already said that the purpose of God according to election stands not of works, but of him that calleth, of children not yet born, neither having done any good or evil. Unconditional election is the doctrine of the text, and it is the confession of the Reformed churches because it is what Paul wrote.

Open theism attacks the doctrine at its root by denying that God exhaustively knows the future at all. Pinnock, Boyd, and Sanders argue for a God who learns as free creatures act, and they are candid that classical foreknowledge must go. What goes with it is Romans 8:29 and the comfort the whole chapter is built to deliver. If God does not certainly know, he cannot certainly predestinate, and the chain from foreknowledge to glorification becomes a hope rather than a guarantee. Paul's conclusion depends on the guarantee: who shall separate us from the love of Christ? The answer is nothing, and the reason is that every link was forged before the world was.
roots_summary: Greek proginosko (G4267), to know beforehand; proorizo (G4309), to mark out beforehand; prognosis (G4268), foreknowledge; summorphos (G4832), conformed to.
roots_lines: Greek proginosko (G4267) — to know before; its object in Romans 8:29 is persons, not facts.
Greek prognosis (G4268) — foreknowledge; joined to elect at 1 Peter 1:2.
Greek proorizo (G4309) — to mark out beforehand, to predestinate; the next link in the chain.
Greek summorphos (G4832) — conformed, of the same form; the end of the predestination.
Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know; used of covenant regard at Amos 3:2, not bare awareness.
usage: “whom he did foreknow” — persons, not foreseen acts.
“conformed to the image of his Son” — the end for which.
“you only have I known of all the families” — the Hebraic sense of knowing.

pos: n. pl. (co-inheritors; those sharing one inheritance equally)
etymology: Greek sugkleronomos, from sun, together with, and kleronomos, an heir — one who inherits jointly. A legal term: not a beneficiary of a separate lesser bequest, but a co-heir of the same estate.
biblical_def: And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together. Paul is reasoning from adoption to inheritance, and he takes the argument further than any reader would dare. Children implies heirs; heirs implies heirs of God — the inheritance is God himself, not merely his gifts. Then comes the phrase that has no parallel: joint-heirs with Christ. Sugkleronomos is a legal word, and it does not describe a servant given a legacy. It describes a co-heir of the same estate, receiving with the other heir and not after him. What Christ inherits by right as the eternal Son, the adopted receive with him by grace. Paul states the whole standing in the plainest terms elsewhere: wherefore thou art no more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ. And he immediately names the condition attached to the joint inheritance, which is also a joint experience — if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together. The two are one path. That is why the very next verse weighs the two against each other and finds no contest: I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under JOINT-HEIR: an heir having a joint interest with another; a coheir.
webster_full: JOINT-HEIR, n. An heir having a joint interest with another; a coheir.
HEIR, n. The man who succeeds or is to succeed another in the possession of property; one who inherits.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; a perpetual or continuing right to an estate.
ADOPTION, n. The receiving as one's own what is not so naturally; the taking of a child of another and treating it as one's own.
GLORIFY, v.t. To make glorious; to exalt to glory, or to celestial happiness.
scriptures: And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together.
Wherefore thou art no more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ.
For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
corruption_summary: Joint-heirship is either inflated into a claim on present prosperity or diluted until adoption means little more than divine goodwill; Scripture makes it a legal standing with a named condition of suffering.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teaching reads joint-heirs with Christ as a title deed to present health and wealth, on the reasoning that the King's heirs should not lack. The verse itself blocks the inference, because Paul attaches the condition in the same breath: if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together. Suffering with Christ is not an unfortunate interruption of the inheritance but the road along which joint-heirs travel to it, and Paul's comparison in the next verse presupposes real present suffering with which the glory is being weighed. An inheritance that pays out now would need no reckoning at all.

The opposite reduction empties adoption of its legal weight, treating it as a warm metaphor for God's kindly disposition. The Reformed confessions have always insisted that adoption is a distinct doctrine with a real change of status, not a figure of speech, and Paul's vocabulary here is drawn straight from inheritance law. The believer is not a favoured servant with expectations; he is a son, and a co-heir of the same estate as the eternal Son. That standing is also the ground of the comfort in this chapter, because an inheritance held jointly with Christ cannot fail unless his does.
roots_summary: Greek sugkleronomos (G4789), a joint-heir; kleronomos (G2818), an heir; huiothesia (G5206), adoption of sons; sumpascho (G4841), to suffer together with.
roots_lines: Greek sugkleronomos (G4789) — a co-heir of the same estate; rendered joint-heirs.
Greek kleronomos (G2818) — an heir; heirs of God, the inheritance being God himself.
Greek huiothesia (G5206) — the placing as a son, adoption; the standing from which the inheritance follows.
Greek sumpascho (G4841) — to suffer with; the condition Paul attaches in the same verse.
Greek sundoxazo (G4888) — to glorify together with; the outcome, its only occurrence.
usage: “heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ” — co-heirs of one estate.
“if so be that we suffer with him” — the condition named in the same verse.
“no more a servant, but a son” — the change of standing.

pos: n. pl. (co-heirs; sharers in the same inheritance)
etymology: Greek sugkleronomos, the same word rendered joint-heirs at Romans 8:17 — a co-inheritor of one estate. At Ephesians 3:6 Paul applies it to the Gentiles, and builds three compound words with sun, together, in a single line.
biblical_def: That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel. This is Paul's statement of the mystery committed to him, and it is built out of three compounds beginning with sun, together: fellowheirs, of the same body, partakers together. The hammering repetition is the point. The Gentiles are not admitted to a secondary status, not attached to Israel as a client people, not offered a lesser covenant. They are co-heirs of the same estate, members of the same body, sharers of the same promise. Paul had described their former condition without softening it: at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world. The distance travelled is the measure of the grace. And he states plainly that this was not known in the same way before: which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men, as it is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. The promise to Abraham always had the nations in view, but the manner of its accomplishment — one body, one inheritance, Jew and Gentile together in Christ — is the mystery now revealed. The conclusion is the church: now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under FELLOW-HEIR: a coheir; one who inherits jointly with another.
webster_full: FELLOW-HEIR, n. A coheir; one entitled to a share of the same inheritance.
FELLOW, n. An associate; a companion; one united with another in the same business or in the same condition.
PARTAKER, n. One who has or takes a part, share or portion in common with others; a sharer.
GENTILE, n. In the scriptures, a pagan; a worshipper of false gods; any person not a Jew or a Christian; a heathen.
MYSTERY, n. A profound secret; something wholly unknown or something kept cautiously concealed, and therefore exciting curiosity.
scriptures: That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel:
Which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men, as it is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit;
That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;
corruption_summary: The one body of Ephesians 3 is divided again either by dispensational schemes that keep two permanent peoples of God, or by theologies that make ethnic identity a standing category within the church.
corruption_paragraphs: Dispensational theology maintains a permanent distinction between Israel and the church as two peoples with two destinies, which is difficult to reconcile with a text whose entire burden is sugkleronomos, sussomos, summetochos — co-heirs, one body, joint partakers. Paul's mystery is not that Gentiles get a parallel arrangement but that the wall is down and there is one new man. The Reformation confessions know nothing of the two-peoples scheme, which entered through Darby and Scofield in the nineteenth century. The dictionary holds one people of God in the covenant of grace, administered differently before Christ and after, with the Gentiles now fellowheirs of the promise made to Abraham.

A more recent division comes from the other direction, where frameworks built on group identity make ethnicity a permanent category of standing within the church — a lens through which believers are to understand one another, with the accompanying vocabulary of centring and platforming. Ephesians 3 dissolves exactly that. The distinction Paul names as the deepest in the ancient world, Jew and Gentile, is not managed or balanced in the church; it is abolished as a ground of standing, because both are in one body by one gospel. Real cultural differences remain and are no sin; a system that reintroduces them as the terms of membership is at odds with the mystery Paul was given.
roots_summary: Greek sugkleronomos (G4789), fellowheir; sussomos (G4954), of the same body; summetochos (G4830), a joint partaker; musterion (G3466), a mystery now revealed.
roots_lines: Greek sugkleronomos (G4789) — a co-heir; rendered fellowheirs here and joint-heirs at Romans 8:17.
Greek sussomos (G4954) — of the same body; its only occurrence in Scripture.
Greek summetochos (G4830) — a joint partaker; used only by Paul, and only in Ephesians.
Greek musterion (G3466) — a secret now disclosed, not a puzzle; the Gentiles made co-heirs.
Greek sumpolites (G4847) — a fellowcitizen; the conclusion at Ephesians 2:19.
usage: “the Gentiles should be fellowheirs” — co-heirs, not a client people.
“of the same body” — one of three compounds meaning together.
“no more strangers and foreigners” — the standing that results.

pos: n. pl. (those who are disciples together)
etymology: Greek summathetes, from sun, together, and mathetes, a learner or disciple. The word occurs once in Scripture, and it is Thomas who speaks to them.
biblical_def: Then said Thomas, which is called Didymus, unto his fellowdisciples, Let us also go, that we may die with him. The setting is the road to Bethany, and the disciples have just tried to talk the Lord out of going: Master, the Jews of late sought to stone thee; and goest thou thither again? Thomas does not dispute their assessment. He agrees that the journey is fatal and proposes to make it anyway. The sentence is usually quoted with a note of gloom, and there is gloom in it, but there is also something the church has been slow to credit. This is the man remembered chiefly for doubting, and here he is the one who says go. He is wrong about the outcome — the journey ends not in the disciples' deaths but in Lazarus's raising, and in the declaration, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live. Thomas had the courage and not the expectation. The single occurrence of summathetes is worth noticing too. He speaks not to colleagues but to fellow disciples — learners together under one Master, which is what the word means. Discipleship in the New Testament is never solitary. Thomas proposes a shared death because he already belonged to a shared following, and the Lord's answer to his later doubt was given in that same company, eight days after, with the doors shut.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under DISCIPLE: a learner; a scholar; one who receives or professes to receive instruction from another.
webster_full: DISCIPLE, n. A learner; a scholar; one who receives or professes to receive instruction from another.
DISCIPLE, n. A follower; an adherent to the doctrines of another; as the disciples of Plato, the disciples of our Saviour.
FELLOW, n. An associate; a companion; one united with another in the same business or condition.
DIDYMUS, n. A twin; the surname of the apostle Thomas.
LEARNER, n. A person who is gaining knowledge from an instructor, or from books or experience.
scriptures: Then said Thomas, which is called Didymus, unto his fellowdisciples, Let us also go, that we may die with him.
His disciples say unto him, Master, the Jews of late sought to stone thee; and goest thou thither again?
Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:
And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together.
corruption_summary: Discipleship is widely privatised into a solitary spiritual programme; the one occurrence of this word makes disciples plural and mutual, learners together under one Master.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word itself is uncontested; what has been lost is the plural in it. Discipleship is now commonly presented as an individual pursuit — a personal walk, a private devotional regimen, a self-directed course of growth with the church as an optional support. Summathetes assumes the opposite. Thomas addresses men who are learning the same thing from the same Master at the same time, and his proposal is that they go together and, if necessary, die together. The New Testament knows no other kind of disciple, which is why almost every command in the epistles is addressed to a congregation in the plural.

The second matter concerns Thomas himself, and it is a caution about how churches remember people. He is fixed in Christian memory as the doubter, on the strength of one week, and the man who said let us also go, that we may die with him is largely forgotten. Scripture is more balanced than its readers. It records the doubt plainly and it records this, and it records the Lord meeting the doubt with evidence rather than rebuke — reach hither thy finger. A congregation that files its members under their worst recorded moment is doing something the Gospels decline to do.
roots_summary: Greek summathetes (G4827), a fellow disciple; mathetes (G3101), a learner; Didumos (G1324), Didymus, a twin; sunapothnesko (G4880), to die together with.
roots_lines: Greek summathetes (G4827) — a fellow disciple; its only occurrence in Scripture.
Greek mathetes (G3101) — a learner, one under instruction; the ordinary New Testament word for a Christian.
Greek Didumos (G1324) — a twin; the surname by which John identifies Thomas.
Greek sunapothnesko (G4880) — to die together with; what Thomas proposed.
Greek anastasis (G386) — resurrection; what the journey actually produced.
usage: “unto his fellowdisciples” — learners together, the word's only appearance.
“Let us also go, that we may die with him” — courage without expectation.
“goest thou thither again?” — the fear Thomas did not dispute.

pos: v. (to send away; to forgive; to release from a debt or charge)
etymology: Greek aphiemi, to send away, to let go, to release — the ordinary New Testament word for forgiving sins. Latin remittere, to send back, to relax, to release from a penalty; the same root gives the English remission.
biblical_def: Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained. The Lord speaks this to the assembled disciples on the evening of the resurrection, having just breathed on them and said, Receive ye the Holy Ghost. The verb remit is the plain word for forgiveness — to send a sin away, to release a man from it — and the question the verse raises is what authority is being given and to whom. Scripture answers it elsewhere without ambiguity: who can forgive sins but God only? No creature remits sin in himself. What the church is given is the declaration of remission on God's terms, which is exactly how the commission is stated in Luke's account of the same period: that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations. The parallel sayings about binding and loosing are given in the same declarative sense, once to Peter and once to the assembled church, which tells against any reading that confines the authority to an ordained class. The Reformed understanding is therefore this: by the preaching of the gospel and the exercise of discipline, the church declares whose sins are forgiven and whose are retained, according to the word of God — and the declaration is authoritative because the word is, not because the minister is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to relax, as intensity; to forgive; to pardon, as a fault or crime; to give up; to surrender.
webster_full: REMIT, v.t. To relax, as intensity; to make less tense or violent.
REMIT, v.t. To forgive; to surrender the right of punishing a crime; as, to remit punishment.
REMIT, v.t. To pardon, as a fault or crime.
REMISSION, n. Forgiveness; pardon; that is, the giving up of the punishment due to a crime.
RETAIN, v.t. To hold or keep in possession; to keep; not to lose or part with.
scriptures: Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained.
And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.
And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.
Verily I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever ye shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.
corruption_summary: The verse is made the charter of a priestly power to absolve, or else emptied of any churchly authority at all; Scripture gives the church a declarative authority exercised by the word.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome builds the sacrament of penance on John 20:23, making a priest the instrumental cause of forgiveness and reserving absolution to the ordained. The Reformation rejected this on biblical grounds and the dictionary holds that judgment. No man forgives sin; the scribes were right that God alone can, and wrong only about who stood before them. The same authority of binding and loosing is given at Matthew 18 to the gathered church, not to an officer, which is fatal to a strictly sacerdotal reading. What the church holds are keys, and a key opens the door it was cut for — it does not decide who may enter. The minister who declares to a penitent that his sins are forgiven speaks truly because the gospel says so, not because he possesses a power to dispense.

The opposite error, common wherever church discipline has collapsed, treats the verse as having no present application, so that no assembly retains anything and membership means nothing in particular. But the Lord gave the second half of the sentence as deliberately as the first. A church that declares the gospel must also, when a professing member persists unrepentant, declare the sober truth that such a life gives no evidence of forgiveness — which is what the New Testament means by retaining. Discipline of that kind is not cruelty; the stated aim throughout is restoration, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.
roots_summary: Greek aphiemi (G863), to send away, to forgive; aphesis (G859), remission or release; krateo (G2902), to hold fast, to retain; deo (G1210) and luo (G3089), to bind and to loose.
roots_lines: Greek aphiemi (G863) — to send away, to release; rendered remit, and forgive throughout the Gospels.
Greek aphesis (G859) — remission, release from bondage; remission of sins preached to all nations.
Greek krateo (G2902) — to hold fast, to retain; the second half of the Lord's sentence.
Greek deo (G1210) — to bind; given to Peter and to the assembled church alike.
Greek luo (G3089) — to loose, to set free; the counterpart of binding.
usage: “whose soever sins ye remit” — a declarative authority, by the word.
“remission of sins should be preached” — the same commission in Luke.
“whatsoever ye shall bind on earth” — given to the church at Matthew 18.

pos: n. (close watching; outward show that can be scrutinised)
etymology: Greek paraterisis, a watching closely, from paratereo, to observe narrowly — the verb used of the Pharisees watching the Lord to see whether he would heal on the sabbath. The word occurs once, and it describes a manner of looking rather than a thing seen.
biblical_def: And when he was demanded of the Pharisees, when the kingdom of God should come, he answered them and said, The kingdom of God cometh not with observation. The question is a question about timing and the answer refuses its premise. Paraterisis is close watching, scrutiny, the kind of attention that keeps a lookout for signs — and the noun is related to the verb Luke uses elsewhere of these same men watching the Lord to catch him out. He tells them the kingdom does not arrive in a form their watching can detect. Then he says where it is: neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you. The Lord is not denying that the kingdom will one day be unmistakable; a few verses later he describes the day of the Son of man as lightning flashing from one part of heaven to the other, visible to all. He is denying that its present coming can be tracked by observers looking for political and territorial signs. His kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight. The disciples themselves had to be corrected on the same point after the resurrection, when they asked whether he would at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel. The question is perennial, and so is the answer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of observing; notice; the act of viewing or noting with attention; a regarding with close scrutiny.
webster_full: OBSERVATION, n. The act of observing, noticing or taking notice; the act of seeing or of fixing the mind upon any thing.
OBSERVATION, n. Notion gained by observing; the faculty of taking notice.
OBSERVE, v.t. To see or behold with some attention; to notice; to regard attentively; to watch.
SCRUTINY, n. Close search; minute inquiry; critical examination.
KINGDOM, n. The territory or country subject to a king; dominion; reign; rule; sovereign power.
scriptures: And when he was demanded of the Pharisees, when the kingdom of God should come, he answered them and said, The kingdom of God cometh not with observation:
Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you.
Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
When they therefore were come together, they asked of him, saying, Lord, wilt thou at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?
corruption_summary: The verse is used both to deny the kingdom any public or future reality and to fuel the sign-watching it was spoken against; the Lord denies that the kingdom's present coming can be tracked, not that it will ever be seen.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberal theology has used Luke 17:20 to reduce the kingdom to an inward disposition — a moral influence in the heart with no future consummation, no visible church, and no returning King. The context forbids it. Within a dozen verses the Lord describes his coming as lightning shining from one part of heaven unto the other, and as a day that will overtake the world as the flood overtook Noah's generation. What is denied is that the kingdom's present arrival answers to the Pharisees' scrutiny; what is affirmed elsewhere, and confessed by the whole church, is a bodily second coming, a final judgment, and a kingdom that will be entirely unmissable.

The opposite and more energetic error is the sign-watching this verse was spoken against. Date-setting, prophecy charts correlating current events with prophetic timetables, and the dispensational system that generates most of them all consist in exactly the paraterisis the Lord ruled out — close watching for the signs by which the kingdom's approach may be tracked. The disciples asked the same kind of question in Acts 1 and were told plainly that it was not for them to know the times or the seasons, and were given work to do instead. A church watching the sky for a schedule is not more expectant than one at its duty; it is disobeying the answer already given.
roots_summary: Greek paraterisis (G3907), close watching; paratereo (G3906), to observe narrowly; basileia (G932), kingdom; entos (G1787), within or among.
roots_lines: Greek paraterisis (G3907) — a narrow watching, scrutiny; its only occurrence in Scripture.
Greek paratereo (G3906) — to watch closely; used of the Pharisees watching to accuse him.
Greek basileia (G932) — kingdom, royal rule; the reign rather than merely the realm.
Greek entos (G1787) — within, in the midst of; rendered within you.
Greek astrapto (G797) — to flash as lightning; how the day of the Son of man will come.
usage: “cometh not with observation” — not detectable by watching for signs.
“Lo here! or, lo there!” — the reports the Lord forbids following.
“wilt thou at this time restore the kingdom” — the disciples asking it again.
